OIL FUNDS wait on sidelines for diplomacy or war

Investors made few changes to petroleum positions for the second week running despite bellicose rhetoric from the United States and Iran and a growing volume of commentary predicting an imminent resumption of hostilities.

Hedge funds and other money managers sold the equivalent of 15 million barrels in the six most important petroleum futures and options contracts over the seven days ending on October 27.

There has not been any significant change in the combined position since the middle of October and arguably since the end of September despite increasingly confident forecasts fighting will resume soon ...

Brent slumps to USD 106

#Commodities:
Oil: Brent trades down 3% with the January contract at USD 110 after trading above USD 114 on Friday. The latest decline came amid reports that President Trump favours giving diplomacy with Iran more time before potentially resuming strikes after Tuesday’s US midterm elections. Qatari and Iranian officials continued talks, although attacks on vessels near the Strait of Hormuz highlighted persistent supply risks. Meanwhile, OPEC+ kept output targets unchanged through December, while Goldman Sachs raised its Brent forecast to USD 105 for December and an average of USD 88 in 2027, citing heightened geopolitical risks in the Middle East and Ukraine.

Precious metals: Gold rebounds 1% to USD 3,915 after Friday’s break below key support, now resistance, at USD 3,970 drove prices to a one-year low, leaving October down 6.8%. The selloff, fuelled by momentum selling and long liquidation, was exacerbated by the rout in AI stocks and rising energy prices. While structural support for gold in our opinion remains intact, market sentiment and positioning may need to stabilise before these drivers regain influence. For now, the focus remains on global equities, Middle East developments, energy prices and US rate expectations. Silver, which led last week’s selloff, rebounds 2.3% to USD 50.20, with traders watching for signs of stabilisation or renewed selling.

Copper trades higher at USD 6.52 following a two-day correction driven by some of the same forces that weighed on precious metals, notably weakness in AI-related stocks that raised doubts about projected data centre demand. While sluggish Chinese manufacturing remains a concern, prices are finding support from growing signs of mine supply constraints. Meanwhile, premiums paid by Chinese importers over LME prices have reached record highs, signalling tightness in the world’s largest copper refining market.
Not an oil tanker but a bulk carrier.

This video, which is making the rounds today, was filmed a few weeks ago in the Gulf of Oman. The vessel shown is not a Qatari LNG tanker but the Kuwaiti crude oil VLCC supertanker KAZIMAH III (9329693), which was struck by the IRGC on 2026-10-01 while transiting the Strait of Hormuz. After a couple of weeks of firefighting, port services managed to extinguish the blaze, which appears to have originated within her engine room. Her cargo of 2 million barrels of crude oil appears to be unaffected. We kept watch throughout.

After 3.5 months at sea, a shipment of 2 million barrels of Iranian crude oil recently arrived in China.
